root_cause.text: `nfc_unregister_device()` in the NFC core called `rfkill_unregister()` while holding `device_lock(&dev->dev)`, creating an ABBA lock inversion with `rfkill_fop_write()`/`nfc_dev_down()` which take `rfkill_global_mutex` first and then need `device_lock()`.
root_cause.evidence: The patch moves `rfkill_unregister()` and `rfkill_destroy()` out of the `device_lock` critical section, storing `dev->rfkill` in a local `rfk` and clearing `dev->rfkill` before unlocking, and the CVE description explicitly shows the deadlock chain: `rfkill_fop_write()` holds `rfkill_global_mutex` then waits on `device_lock`, while `nfc_unregister_device()` holds `device_lock` then waits on `rfkill_global_mutex`.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add a local rfkill pointer in nfc_unregister_device() in preparation for rfkill-related cleanup or handling.
intent_record.what: In nfc_unregister_device(), a new local pointer variable 'struct rfkill *rfk' is declared and initialized to NULL.
intent_record.how: This change by itself does not alter runtime behavior yet; it prepares the function to track an rfkill object, likely for later conditional handling or cleanup within the same function.

intent_record.intent_summary: Move rfkill teardown out of the device lock during NFC device unregister to safely clear state and avoid cleanup under lock.
intent_record.what: In nfc_unregister_device(), the rfkill cleanup was moved out of the device_lock() section: instead of calling rfkill_unregister() and rfkill_destroy() while dev->rfkill is still set, the code now saves dev->rfkill into a local variable rfk, sets dev->rfkill to NULL under the lock, unlocks the device, and then conditionally unregisters and destroys rfk afterward.
intent_record.how: This changes teardown ordering so the device state is cleared while protected by the lock, but the potentially blocking rfkill unregister/destroy operations happen after releasing the device lock. That reduces lock hold time and avoids performing rfkill cleanup while holding the device lock, which can prevent lock contention or lock-order issues during device removal.

relevance_review.reason: The change is in nfc_unregister_device() and introduces rfkill-related handling in the area implicated by the lock inversion. Even though it is only preparatory, it directly relates to the rfkill cleanup path that caused the ABBA deadlock.
The change directly matches the root cause: it moves rfkill teardown out of the device lock during NFC unregister, which addresses the ABBA lock inversion between device_lock and rfkill_global_mutex.

candidates.rationale: This call is the direct trigger for the ABBA inversion: it executes while device_lock(&dev->dev) is held, and rfkill_unregister() can lead into rfkill paths that conflict with rfkill_fop_write()/nfc_dev_down() acquiring rfkill_global_mutex first.
The deadlock arises because rfkill_unregister() is invoked under this lock, so this statement establishes the locking context that makes the inversion possible.

vuln_statements.explanation: This call was made while device_lock(&dev->dev) was held, causing rfkill teardown to occur under the NFC device lock and creating the ABBA lock inversion with rfkill_fop_write()/nfc_dev_down().
This lock acquisition establishes the locking context in which rfkill_unregister(dev->rfkill) ran, enabling the deadlock-prone lock ordering inversion described in the root cause.

Author: Samuel Ortiz <sameo@linux.intel.com>
Date:   Thu Apr 11 11:52:20 2013 +0200

    NFC: RFKILL support
    
    All NFC devices will now get proper RFKILL support as long as they provide
    some dev_up and dev_down hooks. Rfkilling an NFC device will bring it down
    while it is left to userspace to bring it back up when being rfkill unblocked.
    This is very similar to what Bluetooth does.
    
    Acked-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtm
bic_trace_step.reason: The snippet shows the vulnerable pattern in `nfc_unregister_device()`: it calls `rfkill_unregister(dev->rfkill); rfkill_destroy(dev->rfkill);` before later taking `device_lock(&dev->dev)` for `check_presence` teardown. The root cause is an ABBA inversion between `rfkill_unregister()` and paths like `rfkill_fop_write()/nfc_dev_down()` that take `rfkill_global_mutex` first and then need `device_lock()`. Here, the code clearly adds rfkill teardown inside unregister, and there is no special ordering/lock avoidance fix present. The fix is not present because the function does not avoid calling rfkill teardown under the device unregistration path, nor does it defer rfkill cleanup outside the device-lock-sensitive section.
